items.bodyMarkdown: Build practical web engineering judgment through original lessons and real projects.
items.description: JavaScript, TypeScript, React, Node.js, and relational persistence.
targetOutcomes: Build, debug, test, and maintain a web application.

items.title: The web development workflow
items.bodyMarkdown: Trace a request, make focused changes, and debug from evidence.

items.title: Follow a browser request
items.bodyMarkdown:
A support agent clicks a ticket in the browser. The screen changes, but the ticket may have come from a different computer. Understanding that boundary makes debugging much less mysterious.

The browser is the **client**. It presents controls, gathers input, and sends a request. The server receives the request, applies rules, and returns a response. A database is a separate store used by the server; the browser should not receive its credentials.

An HTTP request describes an operation with a method, a path, headers, and sometimes a body. For example, GET /api/tickets/42 asks for a representation of ticket 42. The path identifies the resource; it is not the response data. A response includes a status code, headers, and a body. A 200 response might contain JSON describing the ticket. The browser parses that JSON and renders a component. A 404 response says the resource is unavailable under the API’s policy.

Think of the round trip as a sequence of observable boundaries: a click handler runs; a request leaves the browser; a route matches; the server checks access and reads data; a response arrives; the client updates the display. Each boundary gives you a place to collect evidence. The browser’s Network panel shows the request and response even when the screen itself looks wrong.

The server owns authoritative rules such as access control and persistence. A disabled button improves the experience, but somebody can send a request without that button. The browser owns presentation and immediate feedback. Both sides may validate a title: the browser to help the agent quickly, and the server to protect the stored data.

A successful network request does not prove the UI is correct. If the response contains a title but the page is blank, inspect parsing, state updates, and rendering next. If no request appears, inspect the interaction and client code before changing a database query.
objectives: Separate presentation from authoritative server decisions.
items.workedExampleMarkdown:
~~~http
GET /api/tickets/42 HTTP/1.1
Accept: application/json

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":"42","title":"Printer offline"}
~~~

The request asks for ticket 42. The response status reports success; the final JSON object is the response body. The React component decides how to display its title.
commonMistakes: Calling the request path the response body.
Treating client-side hiding as an authorization check.
Assuming a blank screen always means the server failed.
items.summary: Inspect each boundary separately: input, request, server decision, response, and rendering.

items.title: Use Git and project commands
items.bodyMarkdown:
A ticket feature is ready to save, but your working folder contains both the intended change and an unrelated experiment. Git helps you make the boundary of that change explicit.

Your working tree contains the files you are editing. The staging area describes what the next commit will contain. A commit records that staged snapshot with a message. Saving in an editor does not automatically stage or commit a file. A remote repository is another copy of the history; committing locally does not publish it.

Start with git status to see the working tree and staging state. Read git diff to inspect unstaged changes. Stage only the relevant files, then read git diff --staged before committing. That final review catches debug output, accidental edits, and secrets before they become part of a snapshot. A useful commit message describes the behavior changed, such as “Reject blank ticket titles.”

Project commands are another boundary worth reading. A package.json scripts entry maps a friendly name to an actual command. Running pnpm test only works if the project defines a test script, and the meaning of that script belongs to that repository. A missing-script error is different from a test assertion failure. The first means the command was not configured; the second means the test runner started and observed unexpected behavior.

Use the package manager and lockfile already in the repository. A lockfile records resolved dependency versions so another installation can reproduce them. Avoid switching managers casually or editing a lockfile by hand. Read the README, inspect scripts, install dependencies with the documented command, and run baseline checks before changing code.

When a command fails, preserve its output and exit status. “It did not work” is too broad to guide a repair. “The test script invokes vitest, but that executable is missing after installation failed” identifies a specific dependency problem. A failing baseline is a setup issue to resolve before you interpret the deliberately failing mission tests.
objectives: Distinguish working, staged, and committed changes.
Diagnose a package script failure from its output.
items.workedExampleMarkdown:
~~~sh
git status --short
git diff
git add src/tickets.ts tests/tickets.test.ts
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Reject blank ticket titles"
~~~

Stage a focused change only after inspecting it. The staged diff is what the commit records. A separate push is needed to send the commit to a remote.
commonMistakes: Assuming git add commits a file.
Staging every changed file without inspecting unrelated work.
Treating “missing script” as a failed test assertion.
items.summary: Inspect the working diff, stage the intended change, inspect the staged diff, and then commit. Read project scripts before running them.

items.title: Debug from evidence
items.bodyMarkdown:
A support ticket page crashes only when its optional assignee is missing. A productive investigation starts with what you can observe, not with the first plausible code change.

A stack trace identifies where an error was thrown and the chain of calls that led there. Start with the error message and the first frame in your own code. A library frame may explain the mechanism, but it often is not where your application made the invalid assumption. The trace gives you a location to inspect; it does not establish the original cause by itself.

Reproduce the problem with known inputs. Record what you did, what you expected, and what actually happened. Then reduce the example while preserving the failure. If a hundred-ticket fixture fails, try one unassigned ticket. If a full page crashes, test the formatter that reads assignee.name. A minimal reproduction makes the hypothesis cheaper to test and easier to explain to somebody else.

Choose a hypothesis that can be contradicted by evidence: “The formatter assumes assignee is always present.” Inspect the input at the failing boundary, or add a focused test using an unassigned ticket. If the test fails with the same error, you have strengthened the connection between the assumption and the defect. If it does not, check whether the reproduction omitted an important condition.

Fix the boundary where the assumption is made. If unassigned tickets are valid, represent that state explicitly and return an appropriate label. Do not swallow every exception in the page and pretend rendering succeeded. A broad catch may hide the evidence and leave the user looking at stale data.

After the repair, test both the failing case and a normal assigned ticket. A regression test should fail with the original implementation and pass after the fix. That property is more useful than merely increasing the count of tests. Finally, remove temporary logs that contain personal data and leave a concise explanation of the defect and the evidence that confirmed it.
objectives: Read a stack trace to locate an application assumption.
Design a minimal reproduction and a regression case.
items.workedExampleMarkdown:
~~~text
TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'name')
  at assigneeLabel (src/ticket-view.ts:12:28)
  at renderTicket (src/ticket-view.ts:34:9)
~~~

Inspect the input passed to assigneeLabel. A fixture with assignee: null is a smaller reproduction than the entire dashboard. Test a null assignee and an assigned ticket before considering the repair complete.
commonMistakes: Changing several unrelated components before reproducing the failure.
Assuming the top library stack frame is the root cause.
Catching and ignoring every error instead of handling the supported empty state.
items.summary: Use a reproducible observation, a falsifiable hypothesis, a small test, and a repair at the failing boundary.

hints: Start at the click in the browser.

solution.modelAnswer: The browser sends a request to the API. The server checks access, reads data, and returns a response for the browser to render.
solution.explanationMarkdown: The browser sends a request to the API. The server checks access, reads data, and returns a response for the browser to render.

options.text: Browser → API route → access check and data read → response → render

items.title: Place the ownership check
items.bodyMarkdown: Apply web.request-lifecycle in a support-desk workflow.
items.promptMarkdown: A developer hides Edit for tickets owned by someone else. Explain where an authoritative ownership check must also happen, and why.
hints: Consider a request sent without using this screen.
The API can be called by another client.
Explain server enforcement separately from a convenient hidden button.

solution.modelAnswer: The server must check the authenticated identity against the ticket owner. A direct request can bypass the hidden button.
solution.explanationMarkdown: The server must check the authenticated identity against the ticket owner. A direct request can bypass the hidden button.

criteria: Explain how a direct request bypasses hidden UI.
Preserve the client check as presentation feedback.
grading.modelAnswer: The server must check the authenticated identity against the requested ticket’s owner before reading or changing protected data. Hiding Edit improves the interface but cannot prevent a direct request.

solution.modelAnswer: The failure is at script lookup. Run pnpm test or add an intentionally defined check script; do not infer a product defect from a command that never ran tests.

options.text: Use the documented test script or define the intended check script.

options.explanation: The function has not been tested by this command.

options.text: Ignore the exit code because dependencies installed.
options.explanation: Installation success does not make a missing command valid.

items.title: Explain the regression test
items.bodyMarkdown: Apply workflow.debugging in a support-desk workflow.
items.promptMarkdown: You fixed the formatter to return “Unassigned” for a null assignee. Describe two regression cases and explain how you know the test detects the original defect.
hints: Cover the input that triggered the crash.
Preserve the existing behavior for an assigned ticket.
Show that reverting the repair causes the regression case to fail.

solution.modelAnswer: Test null → Unassigned and a present name → that name. The null case must fail with the original code and pass with the repair.
solution.explanationMarkdown: Test null → Unassigned and a present name → that name. The null case must fail with the original code and pass with the repair.

criteria: Include a null assignee and the expected Unassigned label.
Include a present assignee and its normal label.
State that the null case fails against the original implementation.
grading.modelAnswer: Test null → Unassigned and {name:"Mara"} → Mara. Running the null case against the original property access must throw or fail the expected output; the repaired implementation should pass both.
